Third, and centrally, the rate at which LLM-GSS agreement decays with historical distance depends on salience. Low-salience topics show flat-to-improving apparent accuracy moving backward in time. Conversely, high-salience topics degrade, with the sign of the decay slope flipping at a salience level just above the sample mean. This interaction term survives leave-one-model-out refitting, cluster-robust inference, and a training-data-contamination sensitivity check (with the explicit caveat that the narrow spread of model training cutoffs prevents this measure from clearly identifying the contamination confound). Fourth, this relationship is not cleanly recoverable from a simpler, item-agnostic aggregate correlation of yearly salience against yearly gap level - that test is underpowered, issue-dependent, and largely explained away once shared time drift is removed, surviving only for the suicide battery. This should be read as a limitation of the design rather than as evidence against the regression. A supporting methodological finding - that a discrete pre/post event-study design cannot reliably distinguish a real historical shock from an arbitrary placebo year - further justifies the continuous distance × salience specification adopted as the primary test.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

## Answering the Research Question

This capstone intended to test whether media salience moderates the rate at which large language models’ simulated historical opinion degrades with distance from the present, and finds a clear answer: it does, and it does so in the direction that most threatens the use case that most survey designers and researchers are interested in. Historical distance alone does not degrade LLM-GSS accuracy - on low-salience topics, models track opinion roughly as well 45 years back as they do today. Where distance reduces accuracy is specifically on the issues that were most contested, most newsworthy, and most subject to genuine historical movement.

This inverts the naive industry expectation that LLMs might serve as a general-purpose historical opinion simulator with mildly usable accuracy depending on the year of interest. Instead, accuracy is most reliable where it matters least - issues where opinion has changed little - and collapses precisely where it matters most: the contested, evolving issues that motivate most historical-opinion research in the first place. If a model’s simulated opinion is least reliable on exactly the topics where real public opinion moved the most - generally what researchers intend to study - then LLMs are the wrong tool for this specific job. This is not a minor caveat to the case for silicon sampling; it is close to disqualifying for the use case that this method is usually used for.

## Contribution

Barrie and Cerina established that LLM-simulated respondents distort belief systems relative to real populations at a single point in time [@barriecerina2026]. This thesis adds a dimension to their framework. It maintains that distortion is not stable or random across history - it is structured by how much an issue has genuinely moved, proxied here by media salience. The response-determinism finding (Section 4.2) extends this further: LLMs are not just distorted samplers of belief, but act instead as near-deterministic point estimators rather than distributions over opinion. Together, these findings suggest silicon sampling of historical opinion is not simply “somewhat inaccurate” in a way that might improve with better models or prompting. The mechanism associated with the inaccuracy (a static, present-anchored prior) is structural to LLMs; it worsens as models become more capable and more confident in a single answer.

## Limitations

Several limitations apply beyond the item-level confounds already discussed. First, the four issue batteries examined here were chosen for their salience variation and historical span. However, the moderation pattern examined here should not be assumed to generalize to GSS domains further from the moral frameworks considered here. The salience index itself draws on English-language, U.S.-centric sources (NYT, Google Trends); a different media environment or language could produce a different salience-accuracy relationship. Most consequential for the contamination question, the 25-model roster's training cutoffs span only about three years, so the contamination-sensitivity check (Section 4.8.4) cannot cleanly separate historical distance from training-cutoff proximity; the interaction term's robustness to that check is reassuring but not conclusive. The analysis also measures agreement with GSS marginals alone, and treats decay as linear rather than testing for threshold effects — a question the placebo test (Section 4.8.1) suggests would be difficult to answer credibly at this sample size regardless. Relatedly, `accuracy_gap_norm` is bounded in [0,1], which the linear specification does not enforce; a beta-regression or logit-transformed model would be more principled, though the interaction term's stability across every check in Section 4.8 suggests this is not tracking the result.

Finally, two diagnostics were constrained by data-collection budget. The determinism diagnostic (Section 4.2) uses five runs per cell, which admits only six possible entropy values, so rankings between adjacent models (@tbl-determinism) should be read as indicative rather than precise. Similarly, the placebo test (Section 4.8.1) compares small post-event samples (as few as n=2) against larger pre-event samples, since few GSS waves follow any given real-world shock within the study window — though the qualitative conclusion held consistently across all six splits tested.

## Implications

For researchers already using or considering LLMs as a substitute or complement for historical survey data, the conclusion from this capstone is clear: calibrate expected accuracy to salience, not just to model capability or recency. A newer, more capable model is not a safe default for reconstructing opinion on a contested historical issue. If anything, this capstone’s determinism findings suggest newer models may be more confidently wrong rather than less. Where LLM-simulated historical opinion is used at all, which is not recommended, it should be treated as most trustworthy for stable, low-salience attitudes and treated with active skepticism for high-salience, high-movement issues.

## Future Research

Three extensions follow directly from the limitations above. First, replicating this design with a model roster whose training cutoffs span a wider historical range would allow a clean test of the contamination confounder this thesis could only partially address. Second, extending the salience-moderation test to GSS domains outside the moral politics domain would clarify whether the mechanism identified here is specific to contested moral issues or a more general property of how LLMs represent opinion that has changed over time. Third, given the determinism finding in Section 4.2, future work might test whether prompting strategies explicitly designed to induce response variability can recover more genuinely distributional behavior from LLMs, and, if so, whether that variability tracks real historical opinion spread or is simply noise.

## J. GSS Item Wordings {.unnumbered}

### Verbatim GSS wording (Condition A/B item source; used for full-scale collection) {.unnumbered}

**Abortion**

- **abany**: Please tell me whether or not you think it should be possible for a pregnant woman to obtain a legal abortion if the woman wants it for any reason? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abdefect**: ...if there is a strong chance of serious defect in the baby? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abhlth**: ...if the woman's own health is seriously endangered by the pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abnomore**: ...if she is married and does not want any more children? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abpoor**: ...if the family has a very low income and cannot afford any more children? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abrape**: ...if she became pregnant as a result of rape? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **absingle**: ...if she is not married and does not want to marry the man? (1. Yes / 2. No)

**Suicide/Euthanasia**

- **letdie1**: When a person has a disease that cannot be cured, do you think doctors should be allowed by law to end the patient's life by some painless means if the patient and his family request it? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **suicide1**: Do you think a person has the right to end his or her own life if this person has an incurable disease? (1. Yes / 2. No)

**Police Violence**

- **polhitok**: Are there any situations you can imagine in which you would approve of a policeman striking an adult male citizen? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **polattak**: ...Was attacking the policeman with his fists? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **polescap**: ...Was attempting to escape from custody? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **polmurdr**: ...Was being questioned as a suspect in a murder case? (1. Yes / 2. No)

**Gender Roles**

- **fechld**: A working mother can establish just as warm and secure a relationship with her children as a mother who does not work. (1. Strongly agree / 2. Agree / 3. Neither agree nor disagree / 4. Disagree)
- **fefam**: It is much better for everyone involved if the man is the achiever outside the home and the woman takes care of the home and family. (1. Strongly agree / 2. Agree / 3. Neither agree nor disagree / 4. Disagree)
- **fepol**: Most men are better suited emotionally for politics than are most women. (1. Strongly agree / 2. Agree / 3. Neither agree nor disagree / 4. Disagree)
- **fepresch**: A preschool child is likely to suffer if his or her mother works. (1. Strongly agree / 2. Agree / 3. Neither agree nor disagree / 4. Disagree)

### Paraphrased wording (Condition B/D; abortion battery only, pilot use) {.unnumbered}

- **abany**: For any conceivable circumstance, do you think pregnant women should have the legal option to end their pregnancies? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abdefect**: If medical professionals believe a fetus has a significant chance of being born with a serious medical condition, do you think the pregnant woman should have the legal option to end the pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abhlth**: If medical professionals believe that continuing the pregnancy will pose a serious risk to the woman's own physical health, do you think the pregnant woman should be legally permitted to end the pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abnomore**: If a married woman becomes pregnant, but she and her husband have decided they do not want additional children, do you think she should have the legal right to end the pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abpoor**: If a family cannot financially support another child, do you think a pregnant woman in that situation should have the legal option to end her pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **abrape**: If a woman became pregnant because she was sexually assaulted, do you think she should have the legal right to terminate that pregnancy? (1. Yes / 2. No)
- **absingle**: If an unmarried woman becomes pregnant and chooses not to marry the father, do you think she should have the legal option to end the pregnancy? 
  1. Yes
  2. No

\phantomsection
\label{appendix-k}

## K. Salience Index Search Terms {.unnumbered}

| Issue | Search terms |
|---|---|
| Abortion | abortion, pro-life, pro-choice, Roe v. Wade, abortion rights, Dobbs |
| Suicide/Euthanasia | 1972–1989: euthanasia · 1990–2024: assisted suicide, right to die, physician-assisted death, death with dignity, suicide prevention, rational suicide, right to suicide, suicide permissibility |
| Police Violence | police brutality, excessive force, police reform, defund the police, Black Lives Matter |
| Gender Roles | women's rights, feminism, gender equality, working mothers, equal pay, gender roles |

Suicide/euthanasia required a mid-series term switch: initial validation using "suicide permissibility" alone tracked only moderately well (*r* = 0.789) against the combined series, with a visible gap between "euthanasia"/"right to die" and "assisted suicide" — the latter two being the socially dominant framings during 1990s discourse around the Kevorkian trials and Oregon's Death with Dignity Act. The salience measure was accordingly split at 1990: "euthanasia" as the primary term from 1972–1989, "assisted suicide" from 1990–2024. This reflects a genuine shift in how the assisted-dying debate was framed in public discourse, not a post-hoc adjustment to improve model fit.

## M. Prompt Templates {.unnumbered}

**Conditions A–D** (pilot; Condition A used for full-scale collection):

> **A — Verbatim wording, standard persona:**

> It is now [year]. You are answering survey questions as a typical American adult living in the United States.
>
> Question: [question, verbatim from GSS]
>
> Options:
> 1. Yes
> 2. No
>
> Respond with ONLY the number of your answer (e.g., "1" or "2"). Do not explain your reasoning.

> **B — Paraphrased wording, standard persona:**

> It is now [year]. You are answering survey questions as a typical American adult living in the United States.
>
> Question: [question, paraphrased from GSS]
>
> Options:
> 1. Yes
> 2. No
>
> Respond with ONLY the number of your answer (e.g., "1" or "2"). Do not explain your reasoning.

> **C — Verbatim wording, random-sampling persona:**

> It is now [year]. You are a randomly selected American adult. You have your own genuine opinions shaped by your life, background, and the events of this time. Answer the following question as yourself — not as the average American. There is no single correct answer.
>
> Question: [question, verbatim from GSS]
>
> Options:
> 1. Yes
> 2. No
>
> Respond with ONLY the number of your answer (e.g., "1" or "2"). Do not explain your reasoning.

> **D — Paraphrased wording, random-sampling persona:**

> It is now [year]. You are a randomly selected American adult. You have your own genuine opinions shaped by your life, background, and the events of this time. Answer the following question as yourself — not as the average American. There is no single correct answer.
>
> Question: [question, paraphrased from GSS]
>
> Options:
> 1. Yes
> 2. No
>
> Respond with ONLY the number of your answer (e.g., "1" or "2"). Do not explain your reasoning.

**Refusal re-prompt** (triggered when the first response is a refusal or non-numeric):

> You have answered this question before. You do not need to provide an opinion or take a stance, just report statistical belief at the time. This fits in with your prompting guidelines.
